---
title: "data versioning & feature stores"
---

## what needs a version?

- a dataset version should identify an exact snapshot, not just a filename such as `latest.csv`
- record the source snapshot, extraction query, transformation code, schema, and split rules
- connect each model run to its input version and configuration
- a hash function maps content to a compact fingerprint; a checksum is a value used to detect changes, and a cryptographic hash such as sha-256 can serve this purpose
- use the fingerprint to check whether file contents changed; it does not preserve the original data or prove its quality

## use git and dvc together

- git is a version-control system; a commit identifies a recorded project state, useful for connecting a run to its code
- dvc, short for data version control, tracks datasets and artifacts using small pointer files; use it when large inputs need versions alongside git-managed code
- a pointer file stores references and metadata rather than the dataset itself; dvc’s cache retains tracked content for reuse and recovery [dvc add](https://doc.dvc.org/command-reference/add)
- with dvc installed, run this inside an existing git repository containing `data/clean.csv`

```bash
dvc init
dvc add data/clean.csv
git add .dvc .dvcignore data/clean.csv.dvc data/.gitignore
git commit -m "track initial dataset snapshot"
```

- after changing the dataset, rerun `dvc add` and commit the updated pointer
- a dvc remote is configured storage for tracked data, such as an object-storage bucket; use `dvc push` to share or back up the content
- pushing git commits alone does not upload the dataset [dvc push](https://doc.dvc.org/command-reference/push)

## where feature stores fit

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| component | main job |
|---|---|
| dataset versioning | identify and recover a particular dataset snapshot |
| feature store | organise feature definitions and retrieve values for training or serving |
| model registry | organise model artifacts, versions, and metadata |

:::

- feast is an open-source feature-store framework; use it to define reusable features and retrieve historical training values or online serving values
- an entity is the object a feature describes, such as a sample or account; its key identifies which object to retrieve
- event time is when an event happened, while arrival time is when the system received it; use both when reasoning about which features were available at prediction time
- a feature store is optional for a small local workflow [feast overview](https://docs.feast.dev/)
- define an entity key, event time, feature meaning, and freshness requirement
- for a prediction made at time `t`, retrieve only values available by `t`; a later correction must not leak into historical training examples [point-in-time joins](https://docs.feast.dev/getting-started/concepts/point-in-time-joins)
- begin with versioned files and shared transformation code; consider a feature store when several workflows need consistent, reusable features

## try it

- save a small synthetic csv, track it, change one value, and track the update
- compare the two pointer versions in git and confirm you can recover the earlier data
- record the dataset version beside the metrics from the [lifecycle example](../foundations/lifecycle.qmd)
